title: Garbage collection modes in microservices (server, workstation, containers)
hook: ASP.NET Core defaults to server garbage collection for throughput. Containerized APIs need heap hard limits so the process respects cgroup memory. Dynamic Adaptation To Application Sizes (DATAS) shrinks heaps when load is light.

blocks.text: Workstation garbage collection uses one heap and favors lower pause latency for interactive desktop apps — background GC runs concurrently while the app thread continues. Server garbage collection creates one heap per logical processor for higher throughput in multi-threaded services; collections can run in parallel across heaps. In containers, set GCHeapHardLimit or GCHeapHardLimitPercent so the runtime does not assume all host RAM is available. DATAS (Dynamic Adaptation To Application Sizes, enabled via System.GC.DynamicAdaptationMode) shrinks heaps when load is light and grows under pressure — ideal for variable-traffic APIs.

entries.plainDefinition: Multi-heap GC mode tuned for throughput on multi-core servers.
entries.example: Default for ASP.NET Core on Windows and Linux.

entries.plainDefinition: Single-heap GC mode favoring interactive app responsiveness.
Runtime feature that shrinks or grows GC heaps based on application memory usage.
entries.example: Light-traffic API uses less RAM until load increases.

blocks.text: A Kubernetes pod with a 512 MB limit and no GC heap cap can be OOM-killed while the runtime still thinks it has gigabytes. Calling GC.Collect() in request code rarely helps and often hurts. The knobs that matter: server versus workstation, heap hard limit, latency versus throughput mode, and fixing allocation traps — not manual collection.

blocks.title: Production defaults
blocks.body: Keep server GC for APIs. Set DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimitPercent or runtimeconfig GCHeapHardLimit in containers. Measure with dotnet-counters before changing GCServer or GCLatencyMode.

snippet.label: Compare server vs workstation pause times
snippet.code:
dotnet-counters monitor -p <pid> \
  System.Runtime[time-in-gc,gc-heap-size,% time in gc since last gc]
# Server GC: higher throughput, longer individual pauses on multi-core
# Workstation GC: shorter pauses, lower throughput on many-core hosts
snippet.explanation: Measure pause characteristics before switching GC modes. Server GC trades per-pause latency for aggregate throughput.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Calling GC.Collect() in request handlers. Running workstation GC on a 16-core API pod. Omitting heap limits in memory-constrained containers. Changing GC mode without measuring pause times and throughput.

blocks.text: Server GC allocates one heap per logical processor and can collect heaps in parallel — best for throughput on multi-core ASP.NET hosts. Workstation GC uses a single heap with background/concurrent collection — best for UI apps needing shorter individual pauses. DATAS (Dynamic Adaptation To Application Sizes) lets the runtime shrink heaps during low traffic and expand under load, reducing idle memory in Kubernetes. Container tuning: GCHeapHardLimitPercent caps managed heap relative to cgroup limit. How to prove it in production: dotnet-counters time-in-gc and gc-heap-size before and after enabling DATAS or changing GC mode; fix alloc-rate first.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Longer individual pauses on full GC
Heap growth lag on sudden spikes

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Recommending GC.Collect() in request handlers or workstation GC on a 16-core API without measuring. Strong answer: server GC + container heap limit + DATAS; fix allocations before tuning modes.

interviewTakeaways: Server GC uses one heap per logical processor for throughput; workstation GC uses one heap for lower per-pause latency.
DATAS shrinks heaps under light load — enable via System.GC.DynamicAdaptationMode for variable-traffic APIs.
In Kubernetes, set GCHeapHardLimitPercent to match cgroup memory minus native overhead; never GC.Collect in requests.
60s: ASP.NET defaults server GC. Containers need heap hard limits. DATAS adapts heap size. Fix alloc-rate before changing modes. Never Collect in hot path.
Follow-up: when would you choose workstation GC in a containerized API?
commonPitfalls: GC.Collect() in request handlers — gets you rejected because it forces STW pauses and fights the runtime heuristics.
Strong answer: server GC + heap hard limit + DATAS; measure with dotnet-counters; fix allocation traps first.
No heap limit in Kubernetes — process OOM-killed while GC thinks it has gigabytes.
Switching to workstation GC on a 16-core server without measuring throughput regression.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node uses --max-old-space-size. .NET uses GCHeapHardLimitPercent and respects cgroups in modern runtimes.
Each Node worker has a separate V8 isolate with its own heap — like server GC's per-heap model, but without DATAS or container-aware tuning knobs.
